definition: In this historical philosophical usage, dianoia means rational thought, especially discursive or demonstrative thinking. In the packet, it is contrasted with mere sense on one side and with opinion or seeming on the other as a higher, reason-governed form of thought.

provenance.revision: 1901 New York Macmillan original; archive index checked 2026-10-18
provenance.scope: Source record Opinion (in philosophy); pinned source text

reasons: The packet only explicitly states that *dianoia* is “rational thought” in contrast with “mere sense (aisthesis)” (and intermediate with *doxa*). It does not explicitly define *dianoia* as “especially discursive or demonstrative thinking.”

While the packet says *doxa* “mediates the connection with discursive, or demonstrative, thought,” it does not clearly and explicitly identify that discursive/demonstrative thought as *dianoia* (so the contrast described in the definition is not sufficiently supported by the packet).

The packet does not support the phrasing that *dianoia* is “a higher, reason-governed form of thought.” It does give an ordering relation (between mere sense, *doxa*, and rational thought), but the “higher, reason-governed” characterization is not stated in those terms.
